10.1016_j.ijheatmasstransfer.2026.128705: The diffusivity of a GDL can be determined if its tortuosity is known. However, most tortuosity correlations in the literature were developed for packed beds with various particle shapes, making them unsuitable for GDLs. The few correlations developed for fibrous porous structures, which resemble the GDL microstructure, were typically based solely on porosity. However, porosity alone does not fully capture the microstructure of a GDL, leading to inaccuracies in diffusivity predictions when using existing tortuosity correlations. In this study, a new analytical model is developed to calculate the tortuosity of a GDL by incorporating both porosity and pore size distribution under dry and partially saturated conditions. The inclusion of pore size distribution enables a more accurate estimation of tortuosity, thereby improving the diffusivity predictions. To validate the model, the diffusivity of several GDL samples was measured using a symmetrical modified Loschmidt cell and compared with the model predictions. The results showed good agreement, with a maximum relative difference of 12%. To analyze the water saturation effect on gas diffusivity of GDLs, a new analytical capillary model is also developed. This model calculates the entry pressure for each pore based on its size and geometry, allowing determination of whether a pore is invaded by water. This information is integrated into the diffusivity model to account for the saturation effect. While the model performs well for materials with relatively uniform pore structures, discrepancies at low saturation levels highlight limitations in capturing pore connectivity effects, particularly for GDLs with broad pore size distributions. • Anew analytical model predicts GDL diffusivity using porosity and PSD. • Experimental validation with SMLC shows ≤12% relative difference across GDL types. • An analytical capillary model estimates water invasion and diffusivity impact. • First analytical model to capture gas transport under partial saturation.
10.1016_j.solener.2026.114955: Scaling photoelectrochemical (PEC) hydrogen production technology requires integration with solar concentrators. However, no concentrator has been developed to address the irradiance requirements of PEC reactors. This work presents an algorithm to design a primary optic that delivers uniformly concentrated irradiance on a planar target, such as a photoelectrode. The algorithm can also be extended to different target geometries. The algorithm is demonstrated through a pseudo-2D parametric ray tracing study of 28 design points, considering real-world errors up to 20 mrad. The Pareto-optimal configuration, determined through a parametric study, is developed into a full-scale concentrator and evaluated in a 3D ray tracing study considering realistic optical errors. At combined errors of 8 mrad, the model achieves an optical concentration ratio of 16 at an efficiency of 80 % and a coefficient of variation (CV) of 16.8 % across the entire target. Considering reasonable shading by a PEC reactor frame, a CV of 10 % can be achieved at an efficiency of 69 %. The proposed concentrator, therefore, produces results competitive with more complex solar concentration solutions employing secondary optical stages. In addition, this work reveals the importance of accurately modelling real-world errors when designing solar optics to achieve flux uniformity.
10.1038_s41467-026-74885-1: Sluggish kinetics and shuttle effects hinder high-energy rechargeable sodium-chalcogen batteries, requiring nanostructured positive electrodes with excess conductive additives. Here, we show that an acidic binder-induced corrosion strategy enables activity in bulk S/Se/Te positive electrodes. Carboxylic acid-rich binders create an acidic microenvironment (pH≈3) during processing, triggering spontaneous formation of copper chalcogenide interlayers on Cu current collectors. These interlayers reconstruct into active Cu2X (X = S/Se/Te) catalysts during cycling. Using Na-Se batteries, experimental and DFT analyses confirm Cu2Se reduces the liquid-solid conversion barrier by ~24.1% and accelerates polyselenides conversion. Polar groups in the binders enhance chemisorption, reducing the shuttling effect. Consequently, bulk Se with alginic acid binder achieves 96% theoretical utilization at 0.1 A g‒1, rate capability of 508 mAh g‒1 at 20 A g‒1, stable cyclability at 5 A g‒1 over 16,000 cycles, and low-temperature operation at 0.1 A g‒1 (94% capacity retention at −20 °C). The strategy of transforming binders into active interface modulators provides a generalizable approach for other chalcogens, enabling practical and host-free rechargeable metal batteries with chalcogen positive electrodes. Sodium-chalcogen battery performance is limited by sluggish kinetics and shuttle effects. Here, authors show how acidic binders can corrode Cu collectors to form Cu2X (X = S, Se, Te) catalysts, accelerating conversion and suppressing shuttling, enabling bulk S/Se/Te with high capacity, up to 16000-cycle life, and low-temperature operation.
